newsitem.title: JAPAN: Selling in Japan insurer shares may be temporary.
newsitem.headline: Selling in Japan insurer shares may be temporary.

text.p: Shares in non-life insurers sagged across the board in Monday morning trade, but analysts said the selling triggered by Saturday's settlement of the Japan-U.S. insurance dispute may be short-lived.

"It is likely investors will buy back shares in non-life insurance companies when investors look at their huge unrealised profits (on shareholdings)," said Shinsuke Yauchi, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities & Economics Inc.
"In the coming year, it is likely the sector will generally move in line with the TOPIX index," he said.
The Nikkei non-life insurance sector index fell 35.72 points to 2,353.29 at the end of the morning.

Tokio Marine & Fire Insurance Co Ltd was down 20 yen at 1,120 yen at midday, Mitsui Marine & Fire Insurance Co Ltd was down 14 yen at 636 yen, Sumitomo Marine & Fire Insurance Co Ltd was down 19 yen at 721 yen and Yasuda Fire & Marine Insurance Co Ltd was down 10 yen at 645 yen.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on Saturday reached basic agreement on how Japan should open its insurance industry to foreign competitors.
Under the agreement, the current system of setting premiums for the non-life insurance sector, including auto and fire insurance products, will be liberalised by July 1, 1998.
Analysts said the liberalisation of premiums, particularly for auto insurance products, would be a major blow to the non-life insurance industry, particularly small- to medium-sized firms.

Income from auto insurance policies account for 40 percent to 50 percent of income at non-life insurance companies, and following the liberalisation insurers are expected to compete by cutting premiums to maintain market share, analysts said.
Foreign insurers will likely offer cheaper premiums for auto insurance products by making use of the mail-order service and Japanese insurers are also expected to follow suit, analysts said.
Kouya Hasegawa, an analyst at Nikko Research Centre, said, however, the speed at which the premiums are cut would probably be slow and the reorganisation of the industry would not be too radical.
"The market has been digesting the agreement, and what the market looks at is who will become the winners after the liberalisation," he said.
"In the long term, big non-life insurance companies, such as Tokio Marine, Yasuda and Sumitomo, will probably benefit from the liberalisation as they are ahead in cost-cutting efforts," he said.

Yamaichi's Yauchi agreed, saying that selective buying of non-life insurance companies will appear after investors scrutinise the management policies that each non-life insurance firm has put in place to cope with the changes.
